I am 42 years old and I have been farming for 20 years. I finished middle school, so I can read the labels on fertilizer bags and I listen when the extension agent comes to the village, but at the end of the day I trust what I have seen with my own eyes. My household has four people — my husband works construction in town part of the year, and my son is in high school — so most days it is me and my mother-in-law handling the 10 mu. Some family income comes from off-farm work, which helps with cash, but the farm still has to pay for itself.

I keep about 6.5 mu for wheat and then maize after it. That rotation is our foundation — we need the grain for food and for income, and the straw feeds our animals. The other 3.5 mu I plant with cotton. I spread it this way because if cotton prices drop or the bollworms get bad, I still have the grain crops to fall back on. Twenty years ago my father-in-law farmed this land and he taught me the basics, but I have learned my own lessons. Three years ago I tried to save money on cotton pesticide and lost almost half the crop to aphids — I will not make that mistake again.

For the wheat that is already in the ground from last October, I used improved seed from the county supply store, the same kind I have used for five years. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, and now in early spring I will topdress with urea at jointing if the wheat looks a little yellow. I always irrigate wheat three times — green-up, jointing, and grain filling — because wheat is our main crop and the well water is there, though the electricity for pumping costs money. I spray herbicide once because the weeds come up fast after the first irrigation.

For summer maize, the window is always tight — sometimes only two or three days between wheat harvest and planting. I buy hybrid seed every year because you cannot save hybrid seed. I put all the fertilizer in at once at planting, usually compound fertilizer in the furrow, because there is no time to come back for split application. I irrigate maize twice if the summer is dry, but often the rains help in July. I do a quick no-till planting if the stubble is not too thick, or one pass with the rotary tiller if it is.

For cotton, I plant in late April with an improved variety. Cotton needs a lot of attention — I spray pesticide about twelve times through the season for bollworm, aphids, and mites. It is expensive but skipping even one spray can ruin the crop. I irrigate cotton two or three times, depending on the rain. I rotary till the cotton plot before planting to break up the soil.

I have to watch my costs. Fertilizer prices have gone up, and with my husband's income not always steady, I would rather apply slightly too much than risk a bad year. I hire a little help at harvest time because my mother-in-law's back is not good, but I do most of the spraying and irrigating myself.
